chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In

a man who struck with his sword a camel or a sheep not in its designated slaughter site, and had named (God) when he struck it. He (the Imam) said: 'The eating of a slaughtered animal is not valid if it is not slaughtered at its designated site, if he did so deliberately and his state was not one of necessity. As for if he was compelled to do so and what he intended to slaughter was difficult for him, then there is no objection to that.'
ai.seo_question: Is the meat valid if an animal is slaughtered outside its designated slaughter area?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the validity of dhakāh depends on the slaughterer's intent and circumstances, ruling out deliberate deviation from the proper place (madhbah) while permitting it under duress (idtirar). This distinction highlights the Shia juristic principle that necessity overrides the standard requirement of a designated slaughter site, provided the animal was not already in a state of ease. The ruling underscores the balance between ritual precision and practical flexibility in Islamic dietary laws.
